“The crux of it is how can we create enough real-world data and then seed a simulation with that?” he asked. “Simulators are getting pretty good with taking real-world data, doing the real-to-sim translation, and then permuting the environment to take care of some of these little combinatoric explosions of different parameters. NVIDIA‘s Cosmos environment is actually becoming really good at that.”

There are also limitations to real-world data. Tanner said that human responses for teleoperation or egocentric data capture can be incomplete. If a person in a data-collection scenario drops a knife, for instance, he or she might take a step back and turn off the device thinking they made a mistake, he said.

“We don’t have training data right now where humans and robots are interacting,” noted Tanner. “It’s one area we’re working on in the lab — instrumenting it so multiple agents can work together. We need larger and custom data sets.”

Vicon captures sub-millimeter motion for Innodata

Vicon says its cameras can capture data with submillimeter accuracy and millisecond latency. Source: Innodata

Innodata developed the lab with Vicon, a motion-capture leader that continues to provide technical consulting. The New Jersey lab is equipped with high-precision, low-latency infrared optical tracking cameras that measure movement down to the sub-millimeter level — a degree of accuracy that methods such as wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors and single-camera (monocular) video analysis typically cannot match.

“Plenty of motion-capture companies have discovered humanoid robotics lately,” acknowledged Andrew Knox, managing director of Vicon. “But the teams building the most capable robots keep reaching the same conclusion: If the training data is approximate, the robot will be too.”

“Vicon sets the standard that motion data is measured against,” he said. “Our systems capture people, robots and the objects they handle in the same space, with sub-millimeter accuracy and millisecond latency.”

“That gives you independent ground truth, not an estimate,” explained Knox. “It’s why the leading humanoid developers, frontier AI labs and research universities keep choosing Vicon, and why Innodata’s lab is well placed to become a reference point for the whole physical AI industry.”

Innodata customers can buy data, send in their robots

Innodata customers will be able to purchase motion-capture data in off-the-shelf packages or to commission custom projects. The company claimed that it can produce training data for a wide range of physical AI platforms and retarget motion data from one platform to another as needed.

Customers can also send in robots for evaluation to confirm they perform to customer specifications. Innodata’s experts can measure a robot’s movements and responses in a variety of scripted scenarios, including those in which robots and people interact.

Innodata also provides safety-assurance services to validate robot performance. The company said its physical AI experts apply the same rigorous, multi-stage quality processes that it has honed over decades of delivering premium data for mission-critical use cases in finance, government, and healthcare and, more recently, for frontier AI labs.

Because the lab’s finely calibrated cameras observe each robot from the outside, they provide an external (“exocentric”) check on the robot’s internal (“egocentric”) telemetry, which is often noisy. The resulting measurements can be used to validate a developer’s internal data and performance claims or to provide independent, third-party benchmarks for trust and safety, said Innodata.

“We need to figure out how to do more with less data,” acknowledged Tanner. “In my opinion, that’s going to be one of the hallmarks of the next evolution with robots. We have customers that say, ‘Just give me a million hours of egocentric data doing everything under the sun.'”

“Well, yeah, but you’re going to throw out, according to my metrics, 80% of that data,” he said. “So why do you want a million hours? Why don’t you just want the 200,000 hours that’s actually going to be useful for your VLA? This is one of the areas our our team is looking at with a university partner.”

The post Innodata opens motion-capture lab to help humanoids move more like people appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]> Danish FashionTech startup Rodinia Generation, a developer of clothing production technology, has raised €4 million to finance their industrial phase, including the establishment of a first commercial-scale facility in Portugal, planned for 2027.

The round was led by Vitamin°C, with continued backing from existing investors Climentum Capital and EIFO. This follows a €3 million raise in 2024, as reported by EU-Startups.

“Manufacturing closer to demand has never been more strategically valuable than it is right now,” says Trine Young, founder and CEO of Rodinia Generation. “The brands that produce with us have no need to predict what will sell months in advance. They also don’t need to produce at high volumes to reach better unit economics. They can react to demand in days instead of months, sell more at full price and manage inventory and cash much more efficiently – and on top of all this, they can do so with a much lower environmental footprint.”

Rodinia Generation’s financing comes amid continued European investment in technologies addressing the environmental and manufacturing footprint of textiles and apparel.

In 2026, EU-Startups has reported rounds including €5 million for fellow Copenhagen-based Octarine Bio to industrialise its sustainable pigment platform, €4.2 million for Cambridge-based Sparxell’s plant-based colour technology, €10.3 million for London-based Epoch Biodesign to commercialise textile and nylon recycling, €300k for Malmö-based Salt & Fiber’s seagrass-derived textile fibres, and €26.1 million for Paris-based Syntetica to build a commercial demonstration facility for nylon recycling.

Together with Bristol-based Ponda’s €1.6 million Seed extension, these comparable rounds amount to approximately €47.5 million, rising to around €51.5 million when Rodinia’s latest financing is included.

Lead investor Vitamin°C and existing backer Climentum Capital have also been active in 2026 after announcing first closes of €18 million and €60 million respectively for their climate-focused funds.

“Rodinia is tackling one of the largest industries in the world with a fundamentally different manufacturing model. What attracted us is not sustainability alone, but the potential to change the economics of apparel production by combining automation, flexi bility and local manufacturing at commercial scale,” adds Nathalie Moral, Founding Partner at Vitamin°C.

Founded in 2017, Rodinia Generation operates out of Copenhagen, Denmark and is a technology company founded by entrepreneur Trine Young.

In 2021 the pilot O-Factory opened in Copenhagen demonstrating a new garment production system built on three technology pillars: proprietary software, proprietary machinery, and the ability to selectively integrate external technologies and make them economically useful at industrial scale.

The Copenhagen facility has produced for fashion brands since 2021 and is currently producing the next collections for Henrik Vibskov and Klaus Samsøe.

“We have demonstrated in Copenhagen that a single O-factory line can produce 80% of clothing categories, including evening dresses, formal shirts, football tees, swimwear and​ childrenswear, just to mention a few of the categories that have already achieved competitive margins. The investment allows Rodinia to increase production capacity for existing and new brands with the opening of our industrial-scale O-factory in Portugal,” says Trine.

According to the company, fashion production is becoming increasingly difficult to automate because the industry no longer simply manufactures large quantities of identical products. Today brands need the flexibility to produce thousands of styles, allow for frequent product changes and achieve increasingly shorter production runs at competitive unit economics.

Rodinia’s O-factory is built for this complexity. The technology combines proprietary software and machinery with selected external production technologies, allowing production settings to adapt as the digital input of each garment changes.

Rodinia’s longer-term ambition is a global network of O-factories located closer to the major markets of fashion brands.

“By replicating flexible production capacity across different locations, we are creating the foundation for a new manufacturing infrastructure for the global apparel industry,” adds Trine.

The O-factory is designed to reduce CO₂e emissions by approximately 40% per average garment while eliminating water use from its production process.

Based on Rodinia’s current impact calculations, when O-factories are producing the equivalent of just half the annual garment volume of a large fast-fashion brand, approximately 100 billion litres of water and one million tonnes of CO₂e will be saved every year compared with conventional production.

]]> Zurich-based Namespace, a developer platform that offers fast coding, build, and test environments across Mac, Windows, and Linux, today announced its €37 million ($42 million) Series B to accelerate product development and expand its data centers

The round, closed only seven months after their Series A funding, was led by Scale Venture Partners, with participation from 20VC, NEA, Essence, Burst Capital, and angel investors including Olivier Pomel (CEO of Datadog) – bringing the total raised to €58 million ($65 million). The expansion comes as demand surges, with Namespace’s total revenue growing 8x over the past 12 months.

“I started Namespace because I believe developers deserve better. At Google, I saw how much great tools & infrastructure changes the way developers work. Outside of a handful of companies, that still doesn’t exist,” says Hugo Santos, Founder and CEO of Namespace. “My vision is to make that experience the default for every fast moving company. We’re starting where developers and their agents spend the entire day: coding and CI.”

Namespace’s Series B comes amid continued investment in European developer tooling and infrastructure in 2026.

EU-Startups has covered approximately €160 million in funding across ten comparable or adjacent companies this year, including €61.5 million for Belfast-based software supply-chain platform Cloudsmith, €31 million for Cambridge-based software engineering company Undo, €21 million for Paris-based orchestration platform Kestra, and €4 million for Helsinki-based AI-native CI/CD startup Avrea.

Switzerland has also contributed to this activity, with Zurich-based Rapidata raising €7.2 million for AI development infrastructure and Pfäffikon-based AI Infrastructure Capital AG launching with around €16 million for compute capacity.

“The use of agents in software development challenges the tradeoff assumptions made by prior generations of tooling,” adds Javier Redondo, Partner at Scale Venture Partners. “Namespace is​ the platform that can meet the demand for speed and scalability, while delivering the same reliability and security that engineers have grown accustomed to.”

Founded in 2022, Namespace offers fast coding, build, and test environments across Mac, Windows, and Linux. The company was founded by former Google Principal Engineer Hugo Santos.

While hyperscalers like AWS and GCP optimise for production workloads, Namespace says they optimises for coding, build, and test environments. It designs and deploys its own server racks worldwide, then builds their suite of products on that engineering foundation.

Namespace is already working with over 1000 organisations including SpaceXAI, Ramp, Framer, ElevenLabs, Vanta, Bilt. and Sierra.

“Namespace is the best dev infrastructure tool I’ve used in years. We run everything from our CI to Oz, our cloud agent platform, on Namespace, and I could not recommend it enough,” says Aloke Desai, Head of Product Engineering, Warp

According to the company, some of the most important interactions today happen on an iPhone or a Macbook. Yet almost every infrastructure provider skips Mac, which means a developer’s agent, trying to build an iOS or macOS app for the App Store, has nowhere to build or test it. Coding agents need a Mac at any scale with all the required iOS and macOS developer tooling. This has led to a demand for Namespace’s Mac environments.

With the new funding, Namespace will expand its data centre locations, including its fleet of Mac hardware, and open offices in San Francisco and New York City.

]]> RobCo, a Munich-based robotics startup focused on industrial automation, today announced that it has surpassed an €892.4 million ($1 billion) valuation in a transaction that combines new investment and an employee secondary share sale. The company says its valuation has doubled in nine months. 

Existing investors, including Sequoia, Lightspeed, Greenfield, Kindred, Lingotto, and Promus Ventures, participated in this deal alongside new investors, including Cherry Ventures and European Tech Collective, a group of European technology founders. The announcement did not disclose the transaction’s size or the split between new capital and secondary share sales. Earlier this year, in January, the company raised €89.2 million ($100 million) in a Series C round co-led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Lingotto Innovation. 

“This is an important moment for RobCo, and I cannot think of a better way to mark it than by giving some of the people who built this company the opportunity to realise part of the value they created. There was strong demand to invest in RobCo, so we used that moment to strengthen the company. A billion-dollar valuation is an incredible milestone, but we’re much more excited about what comes next: bringing the next generation of autonomous industrial robotics to factory floors,” said Roman Hölzl, co-founder and CEO of RobCo. 

Founded in 2020 out of the Technical University of Munich, RobCo is a physical AI-driven robotics company developing AI-driven robotic systems that bring learning and autonomy into industrial operations. 

By combining perception, motion planning, and self-learning methods, RobCo states that its platform reduces friction between today’s processes and end-to-end automation. 

At the core of RobCo’s offering is Alfie, a robot purpose-built for the autonomous industrial lifecycle. The company highlighted that Alfie combines perception, reasoning and execution to handle the tasks that have defeated traditional automation for decades: high-mix, unstructured, safety-critical work on real factory floors. Alfie will be commercially launched at RobCoN, its first annual summit, in Munich on March 4th, 2027.

Deployed through a robotics-as-a-service model with zero upfront investment, RobCo helps industrial companies automate manual tasks while minimising operational complexity and risk. The company supports a wide range of industrial workflows, including machine tending, palletising, dispensing, and welding.

RobCo expanded into the United States in 2025 and is doubling down on the country, which is already its fastest-growing market. Its customer operations now span more than a dozen states, which is supported by manufacturing and assembly operations in Austin, Texas, and a lab in San Francisco. The company also notes that its CEO has relocated to the US to personally drive the company’s expansion.

“RobCo is building for a future in which AI doesn’t just reason and generate, but acts in the physical world. The progress the company has made over the past few years is impressive, but we believe this is still the beginning. RobCo has the ambition and technology to fundamentally change how industrial work gets done, and we’re excited to see the company take that vision from Europe to factory floors around the world,” said Luciana Lixandru, Partner at Sequoia Capital.

As announced on Sunday, Munich-based drone company Quantum Systems is set to […]

]]> Two German DefenceTech companies used Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Kyiv this weekend to deepen their links with Ukraine, in a sign of how the country is becoming an increasingly important development and manufacturing base for Europe’s next generation of autonomous defence systems.

As announced on Sunday, Munich-based drone company Quantum Systems is set to have several tens of thousands of interceptor drones financed by Germany under its winter 2026/2027 military assistance package, with the systems to be manufactured in Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Munich-based ARX Robotics and Ukrainian DefenceTech company Roboneers have expanded their existing relationship into a strategic partnership covering the integration and joint development of unmanned ground systems.

The agreements formed part of a broader push during Merz’s 4 October visit to increase German-Ukrainian cooperation in defence technology and production. Germany also announced around €1 billion in additional military assistance during the visit.

For the European startup ecosystem, the notable part is not just the procurement volume. Both deals build on a model in which German capital and industrial capacity are increasingly being combined with Ukrainian engineering, manufacturing and direct operational feedback.

Capital moves into defence

The two agreements also come against a substantial increase in capital flowing into German defence technology.

EU-Startups’ 2026 coverage includes more than €1.2 billion in disclosed funding across Quantum Systems and a group of European companies working in adjacent areas such as autonomous systems, drone operations, aerial intelligence, precision guidance and counter-drone technology.

Germany accounts for most of that total: Quantum Systems raised a €1 billion Series D in July, following a separate €150 million financing package in February, while Hannover-based INLEAP Photonics secured €20 million for laser-based drone defence and Berlin-based SPREAD AI raised €25 million to expand engineering software used across defence, aerospace and heavy industry.

EU-Startups has also followed both companies in the current agreements over several years: Quantum Systems previously raised €160 million and a further €180 million in 2025, while ARX Robotics’ funding history includes a €1.15 million pre-Seed round in 2023, a €9 million Seed round in 2024 and a Series A that reached €42 million in 2025.

The figures point to a German DefenceTech ecosystem in which autonomous platforms and the software, sensing and counter-drone technologies around them are attracting increasingly large pools of private capital.

Production shifts closer to the frontline

Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems develops autonomous aerial systems and accompanying software. Its Ukrainian footprint predates the latest order. Quantum Systems opened a production facility in Ukraine in April 2024, later expanding local manufacturing capacity and its Ukrainian workforce. By February 2025, the company said the site employed 80 people and was preparing to increase that number to 120 while producing locally manufactured Vector reconnaissance drones.

The newly announced interceptor programme pushes that localisation considerably further. The drones were developed by Quantum WIY Industries, part of Quantum Systems’ German-Ukrainian network, and are intended to counter increasingly capable Russian attack drones.

Sven Kruck, Co-CEO of Quantum Systems, said: “Ukraine needs interceptor drones at industrial scale. By expanding production in Ukraine, we can respond faster to the immediate threat while building an industrial capability that will also strengthen Germany and its allies.”

A similar development is taking place on the ground. Founded in Munich in 2022 by former Bundeswehr officers Marc Wietfeld, Maximilian Wied and Stefan Roebel, ARX Robotics develops unmanned ground vehicles and Mithra OS, its software platform for connecting and autonomising military vehicles.

Its partnership with Roboneers is also moving beyond supplying equipment into shared production and development.

In June, the two companies created ARX Industries, a joint venture designed to manufacture the Rys Pro unmanned ground vehicle in Ukraine and Germany. ARX said at the time that the venture aimed to produce several thousand systems in its first year before scaling towards tens of thousands annually.

The new agreement signed in Kyiv extends the relationship into deeper technical integration and joint development.

Marc Wietfeld, CEO ARX Robotics said: “Software-defined unmanned defence solutions are key for landforces on a modern battlefield where every action can be seen by the enemy. Together with Roboneers we provide the Ukrainian forces with a robust but smart UGV fleet at scale and at the same time ensure that the lessons learnt from the battlefield are incorporated into the landsystems development of other western armies.”

A wider innovation pipeline

These partnerships sit within a wider infrastructure being built around Ukrainian defence innovation.

In May, Germany and Ukraine launched Brave Germany, a programme run with Ukraine’s Brave1 defence innovation cluster to provide grants to German and Ukrainian startups working across unmanned systems, AI, communications, laser and missile technologies.

Brave1 said in September that it had awarded more than 1,000 grants since 2023, worth a combined €122 million (UAH 6.2 billion), including support for areas such as interceptor drones and ground robotics.

During his Kyiv visit, Merz explicitly described the relationship as one in which German defence companies learn from Ukraine’s wartime experience while German and Ukrainian businesses establish joint ventures and manufacturing capacity. “German and Ukrainian companies are jointly developing technologies that benefit both countries. That makes us safer and stronger,” he said.

From battlefield to European market

For startups, Ukraine is consequently becoming more than an end market for European defence technology. It is emerging as a place where systems can be developed, manufactured, deployed and iterated in unusually short cycles.

The Quantum Systems and ARX Robotics announcements show what that model can look like at industrial scale: European investment and manufacturing capacity paired with Ukrainian engineering and battlefield experience, with technologies developed for an immediate defence requirement feeding back into the wider European market.

The largest listing in history just told the market, in the blunt language it actually understands, that space is a real asset class and not a rich man’s hobby. Good, this was needed! […]

The post The orbital research economy will be won on standards appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> I watched SpaceX go public with the same mixed feeling I suspect a lot of people in this industry did, relief, mostly. The largest listing in history just told the market, in the blunt language it actually understands, that space is a real asset class and not a rich man’s hobby. Good, this was needed!

The IPO only validated the launch business. The part of the orbital economy focused on real pharmaceutical research in microgravity is still not an industry. It’s a scrapbook of brilliant one-off experiments. And what stands between those two states isn’t another rocket. It’s something far less glamorous: standards.

The science is no longer the question

For those asking “is space-based pharmaceutical research even real?” That question has been out of the way for a while now.

MSD grew crystals of its blockbuster cancer drugs on the International Space Station and ended up with new, more uniform crystal forms. That kind of result matters because better crystals can help extend patent protection on a medicine that brings in tens of billions of dollars a year.

Brazilian geneticist and developmental biologist, Alysson Muotri, has been sending tiny, lab-grown models of human brain tissue to space. In microgravity, these “brain organoids” aged at the molecular level much faster – by about a decade – than they would on Earth. That finding has now helped seed the first clinical trial for a neurological condition built on discoveries made in space.

Arun Sharma flew human heart cells derived from stem cells and watched them self-organise into more mature, better-structured heart tissue in orbit than in any dish on the ground. Meenal Datta from the University of Notre Dame grew mini-tumours alongside immune cells and found they formed more consistent, more realistic cancers in space, with structures that actually mirror the disease in patients.

Catriona Jamieson, UC San Diego Sanford Stem Cell Institute Director, has taken this furthest. Her team saw cancer stem cells in space renew themselves and switch on a key enzyme, ADAR1, far faster than they ever do on Earth. That “fast-forwarded” data now underpins a Phase 1 clinical trial running back on the ground.

This isn’t speculative, evidence shows microgravity gives you biology you cannot get on Earth. And since most drug candidates still die in the clinic, very often because the early models quietly lied to us, better models aren’t a nice-to-have, they’re the whole game. 

Every one of those failures is years of someone’s working life and a few hundred million dollars gone into failed trials. If orbit can move that number even a little, the prize is enormous.

Why pharma still isn’t buying

So here’s the question; if the science is this good, why isn’t every serious pharma already up there?

The uncomfortable answer is that the space community, collectively, have made this work almost impossible to buy. A result you can’t reproduce, validate and compare isn’t an asset to a regulated company, it’s just a nice story. That’s wonderful for a proof of concept, but completely useless the moment a quality director of a biotech company has to put their name on it.

Pharma buys when the hardware is validated, the procedure repeats across operators, and the numbers line up against other numbers. In orbit, we’ve been so busy proving we can run the experiment, that we forgot to make anyone able to trust it.

Space does not need its own rulebook

Now the part where I think this industry is about to make a genuinely expensive mistake.

When you’re doing something that feels this new, there’s an almost irresistible pull to invent new rules for it. A shiny “space-grade” quality framework, a certification with the word “orbital” stamped on it. I understand the instinct, and I think it’s wrong from the point of commercialisation, because the entire value of a microgravity result is that you can hold it up against what we already know. 

Pharma has spent decades and, conservatively, hundreds of billions of dollars, building up data on Earth under a well-established set of rules and standards.

These include GLP and GxP (good laboratory and manufacturing practices), the ICH guidelines that harmonise drug development across regions, USP monographs that define drug quality, ISO/IEC 17025 for testing labs, and the assay‑validation norms already accepted by the FDA and other regulators.

That mountain of data is the benchmark. A result from orbit only means something when you can say it in a language a regulator already speaks: same validated assay, same controls, same quality system as the ground, and isolating the one thing that changed because we took gravity away.

The single difference is the product, not the hardware, not the view. Invent your own separate standard and you cut orbit off from that entire mountain. You generate beautiful data that no regulator has a box for and no research director can line up against anything. 

Standards are how markets get captured

And this is where the boring stuff quietly turns into money. Standards look like compliance paperwork, they’re actually how a market forms and how it gets captured. Trust follows standards, adoption follows trust. 

The winners are simply the platforms people trust without having to think about it. Whoever first runs microgravity research to the same validated, auditable standard, as a good terrestrial contract lab becomes the reference everyone else is measured against, the default in the room. That is a far deeper moat and what a regulated buyer pays a premium for, and then can’t easily walk away from.

So here is the test I would put to any team working in orbit: when the data comes back down, can a research director drop it straight into their existing dataset and compare, with no asterisk, no caveat, no translation layer? Clear that bar and you’ve built a valuable product.

Launch is becoming a solved commodity, securing missions opportunities to perform scientific discovery in space won’t be enough to own the market. It goes to whoever makes orbital research trustworthy, by the standards this industry already lives and breathes, and turns microgravity from a place where remarkable things occasionally happen into a place where reproducible, regulator-ready discovery simply gets done, on demand, on an ordinary Tuesday. 

The people who treat standardisation as the product, and not the annoying paperwork at the end, are the ones who will own this when it grows up.

]]> German AI company Aleph Alpha has launched Kolibri, a specialised large language model (LLM) built for mission-critical applications in public administration and industry.

Referred to as sovereign AI made in Germany and released on 3 October 2026, Aleph Alpha says Kolibri is designed for organisations that require data control, documented compliance, and a model trained to operate natively in German.

“Kolibri demonstrates that we have the talent and expertise in Germany to develop competitive AI models. For us, AI sovereignty means freedom of choice by retaining the ability to build and advance this technology, and giving customers control over how they use it. Our ambition is to bring that capability into everyday operations in industry and public administration,” said Ilhan Scheer, CEO of Aleph Alpha.

Founded in 2019, Aleph Alpha is on a mission to build sovereign, human-centric AI. Along with Mistral, the company has become one of the two European champions challenging frontier labs in the US and China. It employs around 200 people across four locations in Germany, and says its specialised LLMs are used by enterprises and government institutions looking to maintain data sovereignty and build trustworthy AI applications.

Kolibri is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model combining 78 billion total parameters with approximately 3 billion active per token. The model is designed in such a way that instead of activating the entire model during inference, its architecture selectively engages only the relevant parts, a design approach that improves efficiency without compromising on capability. Aleph Alpha says German-language text makes up around 23% of its pre-training data, and it has developed a German-optimised tokeniser that represents German text using fewer tokens to enable faster and more efficient processing of German content.

The model supports agentic workflows, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and native tool calling. In RAG applications, Kolibri is trained to answer questions based on supplied documents and abstain from responding when those documents don’t contain sufficient evidence. In other words, Aleph Alpha claims to have reduced hallucinations in high-stakes settings. It also allows users to adjust the balance between reasoning depth and response speed through built-in reasoning controls.

To meet the compliance and provenance demands of regulated industries and government institutions, Aleph Alpha has screened Kolibri against a blocklist of more than 4.5 million URLs, drawing on sources including the European Commission’s Piracy Watch List. It has also accessed every third-party dataset individually for licence terms, lawful sourcing and adherence to opt-outs. In a technical report, Aleph Alpha has detailed how Kolibri addresses copyright, data protection and EU AI Act requirements, while its licence terms and supporting documents are available on Hugging Face.

Samuel Weinbach, co-founder and co-Chief Research Officer, Aleph Alpha said, “We designed Kolibri around the needs of German-language applications, from a tokeniser optimised for German to training the model to reason in German. For our customers, this is an important step of making AI useful in everyday workflows.” 

The new sovereign AI model, Kolibri, follows the company’s April announcement of an agreement with Canadian AI firm Cohere to build a joint transatlantic sovereign AI company. While the merger is subject to regulatory approval, the two companies officially signed a definitive business agreement last month, announcing that the combined entity will operate globally as Cohere with headquarters, R&D centres, and leadership roles in Canada and Germany.

With Kolibri now available and a merger in the pipeline, Aleph Alpha is not only showing that Europe can build its own large language models but do so without compromising on sovereignty.

The post French cybersecurity startup Fleuret AI raises €4 million to automate penetration testing with AI agents appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Fleuret AI, a Paris-based cybersecurity startup automating penetration testing with agentic AI, has closed a €4 million pre-Seed round to hire AI, software engineering, and offensive security talent and accelerate platform development. 

The round was led by RAISE Ventures, with participation from Auriga Cyber Ventures, Wind Capital, Better Angle, and leading business angels from the cybersecurity world, including Jules Veyrat, co-founder and CEO of Stoïk; Alexandre Andreini, Chief Risk Officer of Stoïk; Eric Fourrier, CEO of GitGuardian; Georges Lotigier, co-founder at Vade; and Olivier Pantaleo and Jean-François Aliotti, the co-founders of Almond. 

“AI has changed the nature of cyberattacks by putting powerful tools within everyone’s reach, often for free. Organisations have to test their security against every attack technique, including the newest. Fleuret built its platform to evolve continuously and stay a step ahead of attackers, with a team that puts AI to work for deep offensive expertise. We are convinced Fleuret can become the reference in offensive security in Europe,” said Thibaut Schlaeppi, co-head of RAISE Ventures. 

Founded in 2026 by Yanis Grigy (CEO) and Augustin Ponsin (CTO), Fleuret combines AI and offensive expertise to make pentesting accessible, continuous, and sovereign. The platform is built to move penetration testing from a one-off audit to continuous security across five pillars: know the exposed systems, identify vulnerabilities, prove they can be exploited, help fix them, and verify they are fixed.

According to the company, companies change their systems every day while security requirements keep rising. It highlighted that under NIS2 in particular, a growing number of organisations have to demonstrate how robust their security is. However, penetration testing still relies largely on one-off audits, which include a snapshot of a system at a given moment, even though a new deployment a few days later can already have changed its attack surface.

Fleuret claims to automate the pentester’s work with two AI agents, Emile and Champollion. They map a company’s environment, explore its applications, APIs and infrastructure, then try to exploit the vulnerabilities they find. It notes that every finding includes a proof of compromise demonstrating how it can be exploited. The platform then keeps watching the attack surface and can trigger new tests as the system changes.

The French startup further notes that, beyond finding vulnerabilities, it is building tools to see them through to resolution: prioritisation by exploitability, integration with the tools engineering teams already use, automatic re-testing, and reports that verify a vulnerability has been fixed.

“We do not simply want to automate penetration testing as it exists today. Our ambition is to build the offensive security layer that will keep companies secure all year round, whatever their size. This round gives us the means to accelerate that vision and to build a platform designed for enterprise environments from day one,” said Grigy, CEO and co-founder of Fleuret. 

The company currently employs about ten people and counts several customers, including Brevo, Stoïk, and Yogosha. “From the start, the ambition is European: make offensive security accessible to every company, including those that cannot afford regular penetration tests,” the company said.

The round also saw participation from PROfounders, Scale Capital, and existing investors. The Series A follows […]

The post Copenhagen’s Pandektes raises €13.5 million to build the data infrastructure for AI-powered legal research appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Pandektes, a Copenhagen-based LegalTech company specialising in legal research, has raised €13.5 million in a Series A funding round.

The round was led by Alstin Capital, a Munich-based early-stage venture capital firm with a focus on B2B software companies. The round also saw participation from PROfounders, Scale Capital, and existing investors. The Series A follows the company’s €2.9 million Seed investment announced last year.

“We have rarely seen a market like legal research, where so many end-users would like to switch their core system but historically simply couldn’t. Pandektes is building a modern data infrastructure for the entire European legal landscape that makes exactly that possible,” said Andreas Schenk, Managing Partner at Alstin Capital.

Founded in 2022 by Casper Laursen and Søren Brokær, Pandektes has built a platform that continuously collects, structures, and connects legal information spanning legislation, court decisions, administrative rulings, and other legal sources, and combines it with an organisation’s own data. The company says the platform gives legal professionals faster, more reliable access to legal research than existing services.

The process of aggregating legal information from thousands of sources, structuring it, and keeping it updated remains complex, which has led to near-monopoly status for local incumbents. Pandektes believes the advancements in AI have fundamentally changed that notion, and its platform is taking on a handful of established players, including LexisNexis, Westlaw, Beck and Karnov.

“Building a serious challenger was always deemed impossible. Today, we can collect and make sense of legal information at a scale that was not feasible before. That fundamentally changes what legal research can be,” said Laursen, co-founder and CEO at Pandektes.

The traction to date suggests Pandektes can move the needle in an industry where switching costs have been high and innovation limited. It is currently active in Denmark, Germany and Switzerland and used by more than 500 law firms, enterprises, and public institutions. The company reports sixfold revenue growth over the past 12 months, and around two-thirds of organisations that trial the platform become paying customers.

Pandektes, however, doesn’t want to be the LegalTech platform replacing legacy research platforms. It wants to be the foundational data layer for any organisation building legal technology by supplying them with accurate and structured legal data through its API.

“We believe the next generation of legal products will only be as good as the data they are built on. To create systems legal professionals can truly trust, that data needs to be structured and optimised from the ground up for AI agents and other AI systems. That is what we work on every day at Pandektes,” added Laursen.

The new capital will be used to expand the company’s footprint across Europe and North America, with the aim of making cross-border legal research consistent and accessible. The company will also use the funding to grow its team and open its technology infrastructure through an API.

]]> Breye Therapeutics (Breye), a Danish clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing oral therapeutics for the early treatment of retinal diseases, has closed an oversubscribed €67.5 million Series A financing round.

The round was co-led by new investor Mission BioCapital and existing investor Novo Holdings, with participation from existing investor Sound Bioventures and additional new investors, including the Ljungström family office, Innovestor Life Science, EIFO, Catalyze Capital, Modi Ventures and Pappas Capital. Together with this financing, Robert Blazej, Partner at Mission BioCapital, and Lukas Ljungström from the Ljungström family office will join Breye’s board.

Ulrik Mouritzen, Chief Executive Officer, Breye Therapeutics, said, “This €67.5 million Series A financing, which includes significant support from both new and existing investors, reflects the strong confidence in Breye’s vision, strategy, and pipeline. It marks a major milestone for the Company and validates the enormous progress we have made to date. Importantly, it enables us to advance danegaptide, our pioneering, first-in-class oral treatment for diabetic retinopathy, to the next stage of clinical development – bringing a much-needed patient-friendly treatment option closer to those living with this debilitating eye disease.”

Breye was founded in 2019 and emerged from stealth in November 2022 after closing a €4 million Seed round led by Novo Holdings and Sound Bioventures. Mouritzen, an M.D. and industry veteran with more than 20 years of R&D, regulatory, and commercial experience in Europe and the US, leads the company.

It is developing a pipeline of oral therapies for eye diseases, such as intermediate age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma. According to the company, diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of vision loss among working-age adults, affecting about 130 million people worldwide today. It also highlighted that the current market value of diabetic retinopathy therapeutics is approaching €8.8 billion ($10 billion), and could nearly double over the next decade, with a predicted CAGR of 6.5%.

“While currently available intravitreal (IVT) treatments can help preserve vision in patients with late-stage disease, their invasive nature – being injected directly into the eye – means they are often poorly tolerated and associated with low continued adherence. In addition, treatment options for patients with early- or moderate-stage Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) remain very limited,” the company mentioned in the press release. 

It opines that this unmet medical need, coupled with a growing patient population, highlights the substantial market opportunity for danegaptide. 

Danegaptide is the company’s lead candidate and a first-in-class oral small molecule with a novel mechanism of action that stabilises retinal vasculature, protecting against retinal capillary breakdown and vascular leakage caused by chronically high glucose levels (hyperglycemia).

Breye reports that the financing follows the successful completion of a Phase 1b trial in patients with NPDR last year, which showed danegaptide was well tolerated across all dose levels and exhibited early signs of clinical activity, including retinal imaging data consistent with reductions in vascular leakage, one of the core pathologies of NPDR.

Recently, Breye also published an academic paper analysing the pre-clinical and early clinical-stage evidence for danegaptide in the prestigious journal Science Translational Medicine.

Robert Blazej, Partner, Mission BioCapital, said, “Breye is emerging as a leader in the development of innovative retinal disease therapies, as demonstrated by the promising results from its recent Phase Ib study of danegaptide, and we are excited to support the Company at this pivotal stage of growth. With its highly differentiated approach, clear development strategy and experienced team, we believe Breye is uniquely positioned to address a significant unmet need in diabetic retinopathy.”

The company plans to use this capital to advance Breye’s lead asset danegaptide into a randomised Phase 2 clinical trial in patients with NPDR. The study, which aims to demonstrate clinical proof of concept, is due to start in 2027.

The funding will also support the company’s broader pipeline of oral small molecules, including a P2X7 receptor antagonist for iAMD intended to reduce nerve damage and inflammation, and additional glaucoma candidates with neuroprotective effects. These are advancing towards IND-enabling studies.

]]> 09aeb322e7719113c31b49defe66628b Fri, 02 Oct 2026 09:05:00 +0200 Juice’s September 2026 Earth flyby: the movie Video: 00:00:48

On 28 September 2026, ESA’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) successfully completed a gravity assist flyby of Earth. Flight controllers guided the spacecraft close to our home planet to increase its velocity by 3.5 km/s and deflect its trajectory by an angle of 20°.

As Juice flew just 8640 km above the Indian Ocean, it snapped a series of images with its onboard monitoring cameras, giving us a unique ‘Juice eye view’ of our home planet.

Juice’s monitoring cameras provide 1024 x 1024 pixel snapshots that can be processed in colour. Their main purpose is to monitor the spacecraft’s various booms and antennas, especially during the challenging period after launch. The photos they captured of Earth during the flyby are a bonus.

In the first seconds of the video we see a view from Juice monitoring camera 2 – or JMC2 – with Earth appearing as a thin crescent at the bottom right of the frame. Around 10 seconds in, we switch to a view from JMC1, with almost the entire disc of Earth visible at the top right of the frame. The large land mass that we see is Africa. Even the Moon is visible as a tiny grey dot to Earth’s right. At the very end of the video, JMC1 gives us a final view of Earth in the distance as it flies away on 29 September.

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><link rel="pingback" href="https://www.studyineurope.eu/xmlrpc.php"> <style id="sie-lean-layout"> #sie-lean-main { margin: 0; }
 #sie-lean-main > *:first-child,
 #sie-lean-main .sie-field-page { margin-top: 0; }
 .et_builder_inner_content { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_section { position: relative; }
 .et_pb_row { position: relative; width: 80%; max-width: 1080px; margin: 0 auto; }
 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;
 margin: 32px 0 40px;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-field-intro-block{margin: 0 0 48px;}
.sie-field-intro-block p{font-size: 17px;
 line-height: 1.78;
 color: #374151;
 margin: 0;
 margin-top:40px;}
.sie-field-section{padding: 64px 0;
 border-bottom: 1px solid #E5E7EB;}
.sie-field-section:last-child{border-bottom: none;}
.sie-field-section-header{margin-bottom: 40px;}
.sie-field-section-header h2{font-size: 32px;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #003B73;
 margin: 0 0 8px;}
.sie-field-section-header p{font-size: 17px;
 color: #003B73;
 margin: 0;}
.sie-breadcrumb{padding: 16px 0 0;}
.sie-breadcrumb__list{display: flex; gap: 8px; list-style: none;
 margin: 0; padding: 0; font-size: 0.85rem; color: #6B7280;
 flex-wrap: wrap;}
.sie-breadcrumb__list li:not(:last-child)::after{content: '/'; margin-left: 8px;}

.sie-dest-panel__globe { font-size:22px; color:#1e66f5; line-height:1; }
.sie-dest-panel__title { font-size:1.5rem; font-weight:800; color:#0b3770; margin:0; line-height:1.2; }
.sie-dest-panel__close { background:transparent; border:0; font-size:22px; color:#0b3770; cursor:pointer; padding:6px 8px; border-radius:8px; line-height:1; opacity:.75; transition:opacity .15s,background .15s; flex-shrink:0; }
.sie-dest-panel__close:hover { opacity:1; background:#f0f4ff; }
.sie-dest-panel__sub { color:#466087; font-size:.94rem; margin:0 0 20px; flex-shrink:0; }
.sie-dest-panel__grid { display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(4,1fr); gap:14px; flex:1; align-content:start; }
@media (max-width:620px){ .sie-dest-panel__grid { grid-template-columns:repeat(2,1fr); gap:10px; } }
@media (min-width:621px) and (max-width:860px){ .sie-dest-panel__grid { grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr); } }
.sie-dest-panel__card { position:relative; display:block; aspect-ratio:3/2; border-radius:12px; overflow:hidden; text-decoration:none; background:#1d3557; }
/* background-image only applies once the panel is open — browsers don't fetch a
 url() sitting unused in a custom property, so the 24 card images (~170KB) cost
 nothing at page load. They fetch on the first SIEDest.open(). */
.sie-dest-panel__card-bg { position:absolute; inset:0; background-size:cover; background-position:center; transition:transform .4s ease; will-change:transform; }
.sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__card-bg { background-image:var(--card-hero); }
.sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg { transform:scale(1.07); }
.sie-dest-panel__card-body { position:absolute; inset:0; display:flex; flex-direction:column; justify-content:flex-end; padding:10px 12px; background:linear-gradient(to top,rgba(0,0,0,.72) 0%,rgba(0,0,0,.30) 55%,transparent 100%); }
.sie-dest-panel__card-name { color:#fff; font-weight:700; font-size:.92rem; line-height:1.2; text-shadow:0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55); display:block; }
.sie-dest-panel__card-arrow { display:block; color:rgba(255,255,255,0); font-size:.75rem; margin-top:2px; transition:color .2s ease,transform .2s ease; line-height:1; }

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<item>
  <title>European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</title>
  <link>https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/news/european-student-card-initiative-at-eaie-2026-in-glasgow-main-highlights</link>
  <description>
<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</h1>
<span><span>holbobe</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2026-09-30T09:11:45+02:00" title="Wednesday, September 30, 2026 - 09:11">Wed, 09/30/2026 - 09:11</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><p>EAIE 2026 took place from 8 to 11 September, with this year’s theme being “The Rhythm of Revolution”. ESCI featured in five activities: two sessions in the main conference programme and three mini-sessions at the European Commission stand.</p><h2>Shaping the next phase of the ESCI</h2><p>The session “What’s next for the European Student Card Initiative?” brought together Victor Aguilar Mendez from the European Commission, Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir from RANNIS and Sergi Martínez Rigol from the University of Barcelona to discuss the roadmap beyond 2027.</p><p>The discussion highlighted three main points:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ec04a08fab5a0a15faf6d0537ff166c1e"><strong>Build on strong foundations</strong>. Participants welcomed the ambition to further simplify student mobility and emphasised the importance of building on the progress already achieved. They also noted that digital transformation involves more than technical connections, requiring aligned processes, staff capacity and resources.</li><li data-list-item-id="ec8f6683d0b4c64c36760e88ede263ada"><strong>Give institutions clarity and time to prepare</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of clear information on the <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/about/esci-2028-2034/continuity-and-preparation?">future scope of ESCI+</a>, practical implications and transition arrangements. The European Commission indicated that 2028 and 2029 are envisaged as transition years.</li><li data-list-item-id="e8a2629faf233a9053a3e7c84c25e2248"><strong>Broaden engagement beyond international relations and IT teams</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of involving university leadership, national authorities, governance bodies and research and education networks.</li></ul><h2>Practical exchange at the European Commission stand</h2><p>Three mini-sessions created space for practical discussion and peer exchange at the European Commission stand:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ea46800eaa0963f636bf8742a636fe844"><strong>Digital Officers and ESCI Champions</strong>: “Meet and Greet” explored different opportunities for close collaboration and participants discussed faster communication channels, technical sub-groups and ways to strengthen the community of practitioners.</li><li data-list-item-id="e722608eb7be29071793748afb04db370"><strong>ESCI+ timeline: what to expect and when</strong>, focused on preparations in 2026 and plans for 2027. Participants asked for timely communication, hands-on training, transition arrangements and support to integrate future developments with existing systems.</li><li data-list-item-id="e4abeb75d22c4e87d628dd3a9174bdc0a"><strong>How to issue your first European Student Card</strong> introduced the practical tools available to card issuers, including the ESC Router and the ESC Service Manager for listing services available to ESC holders.</li></ul><h2>Poster session: “The European Student Card: Bridging borders for students”</h2><p>The poster attracted strong interest, with ESCI representatives Elodie Ham (EACEA) and Deborah Arnold (NTT DATA) engaging with participants on the ESCI components and discussing the implications of the ESCI+ timeline with those already involved in the initiative as well as with potential newcomers.</p><h2>Session by ESCI Champions: “Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+"&nbsp;</h2></div>
<div class="ecl-u-type-bold ecl-u-mb-m">Intro Text</div><div class="eac-hero"><p>We joined more than 7,300 international education professionals from over 100 countries in Glasgow to discuss what comes next for the European Student Card Initiative and share practical guidance with institutions.</p></div>

            <div class="slider-text-wrapp ecl-container right-align">
                                            <div class="slider-text-body eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text">
            <div><p>In addition to the sessions organised by the European Commission, <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/community/esci-champions?">ESCI Champions</a> (Kristin Anderson, University of Galway, Ireland, Katherine Bruun Funch, University of Copenhagen , Denmark, and Dana Rocklin, Stockholm University, Sweden) ran a practical workshop entitled "Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+". The session was very well-attended and enabled participants to share good practices and challenges in using different mobility management systems, including the EWP Dashboard.</p></div>
        </div>
                    <div class="stripe-hero-header img stripe-hero-header__with-slider">

                                </span>
                                                    </div>
                    </div>
                            </div>
            

            </div>
        </div>
    
          


  
<div class="lc-padding-top-half lc-padding-bottom-half lc-background-color-white lc-contained eac-stripe eac-stripe--bg-white" id="paragraph-8350">  <div class="eac-stripe__inner">            <div class="full-html-body">
  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2>Looking ahead</h2><p>Preparation for ESCI+ will continue in close dialogue with all stakeholders via support and user training planned for 2027, helping institutions build on existing progress and prepare for the next phase at a sustainable pace.</p><p>The discussions in Glasgow demonstrated a shared commitment to making student mobility simpler, more connected and more accessible. The next steps will focus on supporting higher education institutions as they continue this work.</p></div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution expresses its commitment to equal access and opportunities to mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
